items.text: Codebase analysis reveals a bug in the existing middleware: `internal/middleware/policy.go` line 189 uses direct string equality for endpoint matching, while `internal/policy/evaluator.go` correctly uses the `internal/match/` glob package. This should be fixed as part of the access control specificity work in Phase 1.

items.topic: Middleware layer architecture: separate files vs single file
items.context: The current `internal/middleware/policy.go` (227 lines) contains the access-only middleware. Adding rate limiting and circuit breaking state machines will significantly expand complexity. The three layers have distinct responsibilities and state (rule cache, token buckets, circuit states).

options.label: Separate files per layer in internal/middleware/
options.rationale: Each file owns its layer: policy_access.go (specificity eval), policy_ratelimit.go (token buckets), policy_circuit.go (state machine). Shared types/config stay in policy.go. Easier to test, review, and reason about independently. Recommended because each layer has distinct state and logic.

options.label: Keep everything in single policy.go
options.rationale: All enforcement logic in one place. Simpler to navigate when the total code is small. But the file will grow to 500+ lines with three state machines.

items.topic: Circuit breaker failure detection: what counts as a failure?
items.context: The circuit breaker needs to count failures toward the threshold to trip open. The middleware wraps the downstream handler, so it can observe the response. The question is what constitutes a 'failure' for circuit breaking purposes. This is the single most important design decision for circuit breaker correctness.

options.label: HTTP 5xx responses only
options.rationale: Standard industry practice. Server errors (500, 502, 503, etc.) indicate the downstream is unhealthy. Client errors (4xx) are caller mistakes, not service failures. Simple, predictable. Recommended as the safe default.

options.label: HTTP 5xx + request timeouts/panics
options.rationale: Catches both explicit errors and infrastructure failures. Requires wrapping the handler with a timeout/panic-recovery layer, adding complexity.

options.label: Configurable per-rule via rule_data JSON field
options.rationale: Most flexible—each circuit breaker rule specifies which status codes count as failures. But adds schema complexity and the flat-column decision (d1 round 1) makes per-rule config harder.

items.topic: Middleware chaining pattern: nested wrapping vs shared context struct
items.context: Three middleware layers need to execute in order (access → rate limit → circuit breaker → handler). Two main Go patterns exist for composing them. The choice affects how early rejections work (access deny should skip rate limit and circuit breaker evaluation).

options.label: Standard nested http.Handler wrapping
options.rationale: Idiomatic Go: `accessMW(rateLimitMW(circuitBreakerMW(handler)))`. Each layer calls next.ServeHTTP only if it passes. Simple, composable, follows stdlib patterns. Each layer is independently testable. Recommended for simplicity and Go-idiomatic style.

options.label: Single middleware with shared PolicyEnforcer struct
options.rationale: One middleware that runs all three checks sequentially with shared state. Slightly more efficient (one mutex lock for rule cache) but couples the layers and makes individual testing harder.

items.topic: State cleanup strategy on snapshot push
items.context: When a full policy snapshot arrives, the middleware atomically replaces its rule cache. But rate limiter token buckets and circuit breaker state are keyed by rule ID. If rules are removed or IDs change in the snapshot, orphaned state accumulates in memory. At current scale (dozens of rules) this is trivial, but the cleanup approach affects correctness.

options.label: Prune on snapshot: delete state for rule IDs not in new snapshot
options.rationale: On every snapshot update, each stateful layer (rate limiter, circuit breaker) iterates its state maps and removes entries whose rule IDs are absent from the new snapshot. O(n) where n = state entries, negligible at current scale. Clean and correct. Recommended.

options.label: Lazy expiry with TTL
options.rationale: Don't actively prune. Instead, state entries expire after a configurable TTL (e.g., 10 minutes of no access). Simpler code but allows stale state to linger.

options.label: No cleanup (accept memory growth)
options.rationale: At dozens of rules, orphaned entries are bytes. Simplest possible approach. Risk: if rule churn is high, state maps grow unbounded.

items.text: The existing broadcaster (internal/policy/broadcaster.go) sends incremental events. Per settled decision d4 from round 1, this needs to change to full snapshot push. The broadcaster interface itself can stay (Subscribe/Unsubscribe/Broadcast), but Broadcast will send the full rule list as a single JSON payload instead of per-rule events. The middleware's ApplyEvent method will be replaced by UpdateRules (which already exists at line 97-102 of policy.go and accepts a full rule slice).
